havenco.story: HavenCo was an internet hosting company based on Sealand, a former wartime sea fort off the English coast whose occupants call it an independent country. Its American founders opposed government censorship of the internet and wanted to keep customers' data on servers beyond the reach of other countries' courts, an arrangement known as a data haven. Michael Bates, son of Sealand's self-styled ruler, set the business up in August 2000 by buying a dormant British company and renaming it HavenCo Limited, so it was registered in the country it hoped to escape. It later moved its registration to Cyprus. Investors included Avi Freedman and Joichi Ito. The company hoped to serve online casinos, pornography distributors and firms wanting records that no court order could reach, and it advertised first-world infrastructure with third-world regulation. Law professor James Grimmelmann, who wrote its history, found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family over management, and he said Sealand had probably nationalized the company, meaning taken it over. He could not sue, because Sealand's monarch headed its courts and going to a foreign court would have undercut the claim that Sealand was independent. The new management banned activities against international law. Operations stopped and the website went offline in November 2008. In 2013 Freedman announced a revival with servers in the European Union and the United States and some stored data on Sealand. No report says the revival succeeded, and the company is listed as defunct.
havenco.mechanism: A business that leaves national law behind still lives under the rules of its host. HavenCo's host was a monarchy whose ruler also ran the courts, and the company could not go to a foreign court without denying that Sealand was independent.
havenco.stopped_by: A dispute with the Bates family, and the dot-com crash, which cut its internet links
havenco.laws: Promised customers freedom to contract as they chose; later rules banned acts against international law
havenco.challenge: No state ever took it to court; Sealand's rulers, its own hosts, took control of it
havenco.cost: Investors hoped for a stock listing worth $500 million; the amount actually raised is not confirmed

knock-john-radio-essex.story: Knock John is one of four naval sea forts Britain built in the Thames Estuary during the Second World War, about 16 kilometres off the Essex coast. In 1965 Roy Bates, a former army major who had built up factories and a fishing fleet after the war, set up an unlicensed radio station called Radio Essex on the abandoned fort, after driving off staff of the rival station Radio City. British broadcasting law could only stop him if the fort lay inside the territorial limit, the three-mile belt of sea a state then fully controlled. Distance for this purpose is measured from a line set by law, which need not follow the shore. Law professor James Grimmelmann's history says that by this measure the fort was about one and a half miles from the coast. The government at first left the offshore stations alone, but enforcement rose after one radio entrepreneur shot another in June 1966. Bates received a summons in September 1966 under the Wireless Telegraphy Act, which banned unlicensed broadcasting, and government files recorded interference from his station as far away as Hungary. On 30 November magistrates found him guilty and fined him £100. His appeal failed in January 1967, when the court held that the fort lay on the landward side of the measured line. He had already shut the station on Christmas Day 1966 and moved to Roughs Tower, a fort farther out, which he would soon declare to be Sealand.
knock-john-radio-essex.mechanism: A country's territorial sea is measured from a line fixed by law, so a fort many kilometres from the beach can still be legally inside it. Bates lost on this measurement and moved to a fort beyond the limit, which became Sealand.
knock-john-radio-essex.stopped_by: British Post Office prosecution under the Wireless Telegraphy Act
knock-john-radio-essex.challenge: Convicted in November 1966; appeal lost in January 1967

radio-390-red-sands.story: Radio 390 was an unlicensed British radio station that played easy-listening music from Red Sands, an abandoned wartime army fort in the Thames Estuary. It started in 1965, after two weak earlier stations on the site had failed. The station could only escape British broadcasting law if the fort lay outside the three-mile territorial limit, the belt of sea a state then fully controlled. In November 1966 a magistrates' court convicted its managers of illegal broadcasting and fined them £100. They appealed, and in December the High Court decided the case, R v Kent Justices ex parte Lye, by two judges to one. It held the fort was inside the limit because the distance could be measured from a low-tide elevation, meaning a sandbank that shows only at low water, under a government order of 1964. Radio 390 came back on the air on 31 December with fresh evidence about the fort's position. Magistrates rejected that evidence in February 1967 and fined the company £200 and its directors £40 each. In May the Post Office won a court order, called an injunction, telling the station to stop. An appeal was refused on 28 July, because a new law, the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act, would close the station by 14 August anyway, and Radio 390 went off the air that day.
radio-390-red-sands.mechanism: The court in R v Kent Justices held that a sandbank visible only at low tide can move the starting line for measuring the territorial sea outward. This brought an offshore fort inside national law without the fort moving.
radio-390-red-sands.stopped_by: British courts and the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act 1967
radio-390-red-sands.challenge: Convicted in 1966 and 1967, ordered by a court to stop, then outlawed
radio-390-red-sands.cost: Fines of £100 in 1966, and of £200 plus £40 per director in 1967

radio-city-shivering-sands.story: Radio City was an unlicensed radio station on Shivering Sands, an abandoned wartime army fort in the Thames Estuary off England. The musician Screaming Lord Sutch started it as Radio Sutch in May 1964, and Reginald Calvert later bought it and renamed it. In June 1966 Calvert was negotiating to sell to a group led by Major Oliver Smedley, who was behind another offshore station, Radio Atlanta. The talks broke down in a dispute over a transmitter Smedley had supplied. At 3 a.m. on 20 June seamen sent by Smedley boarded the fort and took it from the disc jockeys. The next evening Calvert went to Smedley's home and was shot dead there. Smedley was charged with murder and cleared on grounds of self-defence. The shooting was widely reported, and law professor James Grimmelmann's history of the period says it turned public feeling against the stations and led the government to step up enforcement of the Wireless Telegraphy Act, which banned unlicensed broadcasting. Other offshore stations, including Roy Bates's Radio Essex, were then prosecuted. Radio City made its last broadcast on 8 February 1967.
radio-city-shivering-sands.mechanism: Offshore forts were lightly policed until a killing over one of them made the issue political, and the government then began enforcing broadcasting law against the forts.
radio-city-shivering-sands.challenge: No legal challenge by the station

rem-island.story: REM Island is a steel platform built in 1964 to broadcast commercial radio and television to the Netherlands from the North Sea. At the time the Dutch had one television channel, shared among public broadcasters, and advertising on it was banned. A company called REM saw a market for advertising, so it had a platform built in the harbour of Cork, Ireland, towed it to a spot about 10 kilometres off Noordwijk and fixed it to the seabed in cement. It was the first European pirate station on a purpose-built structure, since earlier ones used ships. Broadcasts began in August 1964 and aimed at about 750,000 television sets, with advertising and imported American and British series. Dutch law banned such broadcasts, but the platform stood outside territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls, so officials had no power to act. On 12 December 1964 the government passed a law that divided the North Sea into national sections and declared the seabed under the structure Dutch territory. Five days later Dutch marines boarded the platform and ended transmissions. A year later the company's successor returned legally as the public broadcaster TROS. The government later used the platform to measure sea temperature and salt levels. It was dismantled in 2006 and has been a restaurant in Amsterdam's harbour since 2011.
rem-island.mechanism: A state can reach a structure beyond its territorial sea by claiming the seabed the structure stands on. Anything fixed to that seabed then falls under the coastal state's law.
rem-island.stopped_by: A Dutch law aimed at the platform, enforced by Dutch marines
rem-island.challenge: No. Marines boarded five days after the law passed
rem-island.why: Dropped the exact start dates: the two listed Wikipedia pages disagree (REM Island gives tests from 12 August and regular broadcasts from 15 August; TV Noordzee gives tests from 15 August and regular shows from 1 September).

rose-island.story: The Republic of Rose Island was a platform in the Adriatic Sea, nearly 12 kilometres off Rimini, Italy, whose builder declared it an independent country. Giorgio Rosa, an engineer from Bologna who enjoyed engineering experiments and disliked property bureaucracy, conceived it in 1958 and placed it a few hundred metres outside Italian territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls. It was a 400-square-metre deck on nine pylons. Late in 1966 the Rimini harbour office asked him to stop work, partly because nearby areas were leased to the state energy company ENI. He carried on and opened to visitors in summer 1967, with a bar, restaurant, nightclub, shop and post office. On 1 May 1968 he declared independence, with himself as president and Esperanto as the language. Italian officials suspected a way to avoid tax on tourist income. On 26 June police and tax officers took control and blockaded the platform, with only a guard and his partner aboard. Rosa telegraphed President Saragat and got no reply. In August the merchant marine ministry ordered demolition, and his appeal failed. The platform survived two explosive charges in February 1969, and a storm sank it on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, then held the claims of independence unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad. A 2020 Netflix film, Rose Island, tells the story.
rose-island.mechanism: Italy's Council of State reasoned from the builder's nationality. A citizen who builds a platform outside territorial waters remains under his own country's law, whatever he declares.
rose-island.pop: A guard and his partner were aboard when police arrived
rose-island.currency: The mill, shown on stamps; no coins or notes are known
rose-island.challenge: Seized after eight weeks and demolished; Italy's Council of State rejected the claim of sovereignty

sealand.story: Sealand is a former British sea fort in the North Sea whose occupants have claimed since 1967 that it is an independent country. The fort, Roughs Tower, was built during the Second World War about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk and 7 off Essex, then outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea, the coastal belt a state fully controls. Roy Bates, a former army major, had just been convicted for running a pirate radio station on a fort inside the limit. He moved to Roughs Tower at the end of 1966, took it from Radio Caroline staff, and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. In May 1968 his son Michael fired a pistol near a boat servicing a navigation buoy, and both were taken to court. A judge at Chelmsford ruled that October that Parliament had never extended the firearms law that far. In 1978 a court in Cologne refused a request by Alexander Achenbach, a German who called himself its prime minister, to drop his German citizenship, holding that Sealand was no state. That August Achenbach's lawyer Gernot Pütz seized the platform. The Bateses retook it by helicopter and fined Pütz 75,000 Deutsche Marks. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which now covers the tower. A fire in 2006 sent one person to hospital, and a 2007 attempt by The Pirate Bay file-sharing site to buy the fort failed. Roy Bates died in 2012. Michael now lives in England, and the family sells noble titles and a $10-a-month online citizenship while one caretaker lives on the fort.
sealand.mechanism: The 1968 English ruling decided only that criminal law had not been extended as far as the tower. Sealand reads it as recognition, while the Cologne court applied the usual test for a state (territory, population and government) and found Sealand did not meet it.
sealand.challenge: Still occupied. An English court said in 1968 that it had no power over the tower, and a Cologne court held in 1978 that Sealand is no state
sealand.recognition: None. The Bates family says Britain and Germany have recognised it in practice; neither government accepts this

sunk-head-fort.story: Sunk Head was a Royal Navy sea fort, placed about 18 kilometres off the Essex coast in June 1942 as one of the Second World War's Maunsell forts, named after their designer Guy Maunsell. The navy left it in 1945 and stopped maintaining it in 1956. Unlike some of its sister forts, it stood clearly outside British territorial waters, the same kind of site as the nearby Roughs fort, where Sealand would soon be declared. A few enthusiasts ran a small station called Radio Tower from it for some months. When the law banning offshore broadcasting took effect in August 1967, the government wanted no broadcaster moving in. On 18 August a party of Royal Engineers, the British army's construction and demolition specialists, boarded from a tug, weakened the structure with cutting torches and set 3,200 pounds of explosives. They blew up the fort on 21 August. Only stumps of its legs remain, about 20 feet high.
sunk-head-fort.mechanism: A state that built a structure outside its own waters can demolish it, which leaves any later occupier with nothing to stand on.
sunk-head-fort.recognition: None sought; a British military fort outside British waters at the time
sunk-head-fort.stopped_by: Demolished by the Royal Engineers on 21 August 1967

itu-haps-definition.story: This is a definition, kept by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the United Nations agency in Geneva that deals with radio frequencies. It describes a high-altitude platform station as a radio station on an object flying at 20 to 50 kilometres, at a specified, fixed point relative to the Earth. The wording is in the ITU Radio Regulations at paragraph 1.66A. This height is above the highest band of controlled airspace in the United States, called Class A, which ends at 60,000 feet (about 18 kilometres). Projects in this height band include the Airbus Zephyr, the BAE PHASA-35, the Kea Atmos Mk1 and the Stratobus airship. The definition covers radio use only. It gives no rule on who owns the air at that height.
itu-haps-definition.mechanism: This is a radio rule and says nothing about who owns the air at 20 to 50 kilometres. Having a place in the radio regulations gives a platform no claim to territory.

sky-cruise.story: Sky Cruise is an idea for a giant nuclear-powered flying hotel, shown in an animated video that Hashem Al-Ghaili released in mid-2022. The original design came from art director Tony Holmsten, who drew it over a decade earlier. It would carry up to 5,000 people and stay in the air for years, with passengers and supplies arriving from airports around the world on commercial and private jets that land on it. Al-Ghaili suggested that small nuclear reactors expected in the 2030s might power it. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly at all, and Al-Ghaili himself stressed that it is only a concept. No such aircraft has been built.
sky-cruise.mechanism: An aircraft that never landed would still depend on jets flying from licensed airports, and the question of which country it was registered in would remain.

set.anchor: No base has been named, so it has no location on the ground.

sky-cruise.why: Anchor text reworded to remove research narration.

stratobus.story: Stratobus is a robotic airship designed to hover about 20 kilometres above the ground, higher than the jet stream and regular air traffic. It is being developed by the French space company Thales Alenia Space, and the French Ministry of Industry selected it for a national industrial programme. In 2015 Thales described a craft 100 metres long, weighing about 5 tons, able to carry up to 250 kilograms of equipment for five years with a couple of days a year on the ground for maintenance. It planned a prototype in 2018 or 2019 and commercial sale around 2020, and it said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation. Those dates passed. Janes later reported a French defence concept study for a larger design 115 metres long. In September 2025 Reuters quoted the head of Stratobus describing a balloon 142 metres long, and Aviation Week reported that the company had started building two reduced-scale test models. The aim is to be ready for use by 2031. No plans for people aboard have been reported.
stratobus.mechanism: The airship needs certification and flight authorisation before it can fly, so a government controls it from the start, long before anyone asks who governs the air at that height.

set.anchor: Cannes, France, home of Thales Alenia Space.

stratobus.why: Status changed from operating to never-built: only reduced-scale test models were under construction as of September 2025, and the entry already has built=false. Anchor text reworded to remove research narration.

adiz-high-seas.story: An air defense identification zone is a stretch of sky beyond a country's own airspace in which that country, by its own declaration, requires aircraft to identify themselves and report. The United States created the first on 27 December 1950, during the Korean War, because it wanted early warning of a Soviet air attack. About 20 countries and regions now have such zones, including Canada, India, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom. American policy applies its zone only to commercial aircraft intending to enter American airspace. On 23 November 2013 China declared a zone over the East China Sea, with reporting duties for aircraft as far as 300 miles from its territorial waters and over islands Japan controls. Japan warned of unpredictable events, and the United States objected too. South Korea then expanded its own zone so that it partly overlapped those of China and Japan. Legal writers disagree about the practice. One view holds that a country breaks no law by declaring a zone, and another says the zones conflict with freedom of navigation in international airspace. No treaty authorises them, and Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore noted in 2014 that global conventions do not expressly forbid them either. They remain in use, and China's zone is still declared.
adiz-high-seas.mechanism: A state can extend practical control over the air above the open ocean by imposing reporting rules, without claiming to own that air. Whether this is lawful remains disputed.
adiz-high-seas.laws: Each country sets its own rules, which require aircraft to report
adiz-high-seas.challenge: Japan and the United States objected in 2013; China's zone remains declared

tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.story: The Tokyo Convention is a treaty signed in Tokyo on 14 September 1963 that settles which country's law applies inside an aircraft in flight, including over the open ocean or anywhere else outside every state's territory. It does not cover state aircraft used for military, customs or police work. The answer it gives is the state of registration, meaning the country where the aircraft is listed. That country has power over crimes committed on board, and every party to the treaty must make sure its law provides for this. The treaty lets a commander, the crew and in some cases passengers act to prevent offences, and the commander may put an offender off the plane or hand them to the authorities on landing. Other states generally may not interfere with an aircraft in flight to enforce their criminal law, with some exceptions. The arrangement resembles the rule for ships, which fall under the law of the country whose flag they fly. An article in India's NLIU Law Review describes jurisdiction, meaning legal authority, as resting first with the country of registration, with other countries sharing some powers. An aircraft flying over land no state owns therefore still carries a national legal system with it, and a registered flying platform would too.
tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.mechanism: Registering an aircraft attaches one country's law to it, even over places no state owns. An aircraft cannot escape national law simply by flying somewhere outside every country.
tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.laws: The country of registration has legal power over crimes on board; the commander may restrain offenders and put them off the plane

chicago-convention.story: The Chicago Convention is the main treaty on international civil aviation. Fifty-two states signed it in Chicago on 7 December 1944, and it came into force on 4 April 1947, the same day the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations aviation agency, began work. Article 1 says every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the airspace above its territory. This continues a rule in the 1919 Paris Convention on air travel, and scholars trace both to an old Roman-law saying that whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky. Under the 1982 law of the sea treaty, a state's airspace also covers the air above its territorial waters, the coastal belt it fully controls. Over the open ocean beyond that belt, the rules are those set under the Chicago Convention itself. The treaty never says how high a state's sovereignty goes, and no later agreement has settled the height. Balloon flights, space planes and proposals for floating cities therefore keep raising the same question. Any self-governing place in the air above a state's land or territorial waters would have to start from this text. The treaty remains in force.
chicago-convention.mechanism: Airspace is treated as part of a country's territory. The air above a state's land or territorial waters already belongs to that state, so no new country can be set up there without its consent.
chicago-convention.laws: Article 1 gives each state complete and exclusive authority over the airspace above its territory
chicago-convention.recognition: Treaty in force since 1947; it created the United Nations civil aviation agency

us-v-causby.story: United States v. Causby is a 1946 decision of the American Supreme Court on whether a landowner owns the sky above their land. The Causby family had 2.8 acres near an airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina, with a house and buildings used mainly for raising chickens. The end of a runway lay 2,220 feet from their barn. American military bombers, transports and fighters used the airport, and their low, frequent flights passed over the land. The family argued that this amounted to the government taking their property, which under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution requires payment. A lower court, the Court of Claims, agreed. The Supreme Court then had to deal with an old common-law rule, written in Latin as cujus est solum ejus est usque ad coelum, meaning that whoever owns the soil owns everything up to the sky. The Court wrote that this doctrine has no place in the modern world and that the air is a public highway, as Congress had declared. If the old rule stood, every transcontinental flight would expose its operator to countless trespass suits. So the sky was not the family's to own, though flights low enough to interfere with the use of their land could still count as a taking.
us-v-causby.mechanism: Ownership of land does not extend indefinitely upward. A landowner has rights only in the low air needed to use the land, and so cannot found a private domain in the sky above it.
us-v-causby.stopped_by: The Supreme Court, which rejected ownership of the sky above land
us-v-causby.challenge: The claim to own the sky lost; the family kept a narrower claim for low flights over their land

antarctic-claims-article-iv.story: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, in eight separate claims, and a treaty has frozen all of them since 1961. France dates its claim to Adélie Land from 1840. Britain's claim dates to 1908, when it said it needed to regulate and tax whaling. New Zealand followed in 1923, Australia in 1933, Norway with Peter I Island in 1931 and Queen Maud Land in 1939, Chile in 1940 and Argentina in the 1940s. The claims of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap, and in 1943 Britain began Operation Tabarin to put people on the ground and support its position. Twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959, and it now has 58 parties. Its Article IV settles the dispute by pausing it. Nothing done while the treaty is in force can support or deny a claim or create rights of sovereignty, meaning legal ownership by a state, and no new claim or enlargement can be made. Countries outside the seven do not recognise the claims, while the United States and Russia keep the right to make claims of their own. Countries without claims, such as China and India, run research stations on land others claim. Marie Byrd Land, about 1.6 million square kilometres, remains unclaimed.
antarctic-claims-article-iv.mechanism: A treaty can freeze a dispute over territory. Under Article IV all sides keep their positions, and nothing done during the freeze counts for or against them.
antarctic-claims-article-iv.pop: Research staff who come and go, plus small family settlements
antarctic-claims-article-iv.challenge: Claims are frozen, neither ended nor accepted
antarctic-claims-article-iv.recognition: Other states do not recognise the claims; the United States and Russia keep the right to make their own
antarctic-claims-article-iv.why: Story omitted France and said Britain was first. The Wikipedia table of claims dates France's claim to 1840, so France is added and the start year moved from 1908 to 1840.

esperanza-base-births.story: Esperanza Base is an Argentine research station near the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, where Emilio Palma, whom most sources consider the first person born on the Antarctic mainland, was born in 1978. Chile and Britain also claim the land. Argentina built the base in 1953, a year after the Hope Bay incident at the same spot, when an Argentine party fired a machine gun over the heads of a British team, reportedly the only shots fired in anger on the continent. In late 1977 Silvia Morella de Palma, seven months pregnant and the wife of the army detachment's commander, was flown to the base. Her son was born on 7 January 1978, weighing 3.4 kilograms. ExplorersWeb describes the flight as part of an Argentine initiative to strengthen its territorial presence, and says he was also entitled to British overseas citizenship because Britain claims the area too. Marisa Delgado was born there in May of the same year. Some sources count 11 births in Antarctica, eight at Esperanza and three at Chile's Frei base. The base now has a school, founded in 1978, and a civil register that records births and marriages. Under Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty, which froze all land claims, none of this can build a legal claim.
esperanza-base-births.mechanism: Births and civil registers are classic evidence that a state governs a piece of land. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says acts done while the treaty is in force cannot support a claim, so they add nothing to Argentina's.
esperanza-base-births.laws: An Argentine civil register office and a provincial school
esperanza-base-births.challenge: Not challenged directly; Chile and Britain also claim the land

villa-las-estrellas.story: Villa Las Estrellas is a small Chilean settlement for civilians on King George Island off the Antarctic Peninsula, attached to the Eduardo Frei air base. Families moved in on 15 February 1984 and it was formally founded that April, with a school opening the same day. It later gained a civil registry, post office, bank, library and church, and 14 family homes stand there. Chile treats it as part of the commune of Antartica in its southern Magallanes region, while Argentina and Britain also claim the land. The settlement was part of how Chile showed it governed the area. Juan Pablo Camacho, born there in November 1984, was the first Chilean born in Antarctic territory, and at a ceremony in the presidential palace the country's ruler Augusto Pinochet gave him life insurance and funding for his studies. The local radio station is named Radio Soberania, meaning sovereignty. BBC Future reported in 2018 that residents on long stays have their appendix removed before coming, since the nearest major hospital is over 1,000 kilometres away. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says nothing done there can strengthen a claim. It remains inhabited, with about 150 people in summer and 80 in winter.
villa-las-estrellas.mechanism: Families, a school and a civil registry are normal evidence that a state governs a place. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says they cannot add to Chile's legal claim while the treaty lasts.
villa-las-estrellas.challenge: Not challenged directly; Argentina and Britain also claim the land

world-park-base.story: World Park Base was a year-round camp that the environmental group Greenpeace ran at Cape Evans on Ross Island, Antarctica, from 1987 to 1992, in the part of the continent New Zealand claims. It remains the only non-government year-round base there has been. Greenpeace wanted a voice at meetings of the countries that run Antarctica under the Antarctic Treaty, and allies to stop mineral extraction and make the continent a protected World Park. Those countries were then negotiating a treaty that would have allowed regulated mining. A British Antarctic Survey account says Greenpeace and other groups challenged them with unprecedented public scrutiny in the 1980s. Australia and France withdrew from the mining treaty, and it failed to gain enough support by its deadline of 25 November 1989. A new environmental protocol was agreed in 1991 and came into force in 1998. With that aim met, Greenpeace closed the base in 1991 and removed it in 1991-92. A study in the journal Polar Record estimated total fuel spills at under 200 litres, with contamination in one spot reaching 70 centimetres into the frozen ground. Treaty governments had officially ignored the base and given it no help, though New Zealand would have helped in an emergency.
world-park-base.mechanism: A private group gained political influence in Antarctica by occupying a site and campaigning from it, without claiming any land.
world-park-base.stopped_by: Greenpeace itself closed it in 1991 and removed it in 1991-92
world-park-base.laws: None of its own; it stood in New Zealand's claimed Ross Dependency
world-park-base.challenge: Not challenged by force; treaty states were reported to ignore it

flandrensis.story: The Grand Duchy of Flandrensis is a self-declared country with no people on its land, a kind of hobby state called a micronation. It claims five islands off West Antarctica: Siple, Cherry, Maher, Pranke and Carney. Niels Vermeersch of Belgium started it on 4 September 2008 as a two-week hobby, drawing on the medieval County of Flanders. It grew to have identity cards, a currency, a newspaper, a constitution, an anthem and a football team, and until 2014 it ran partly as a political simulation with parties and yearly elections. It has since described itself as an ecological project to draw attention to melting ice. In 2021 it registered in Belgium as a non-profit and counted 741 citizens of 71 nationalities. It says it does not seek diplomatic recognition, meaning acceptance by real governments, and does not intend to visit its islands. Its founder spoke at the ChangeNOW climate summit in Paris in 2022, and the project co-hosted the first European MicroCon, a micronation meeting, at Ypres in August 2023. That is its most recent reported activity.
flandrensis.mechanism: A claim to land no one can live on can serve as publicity for conservation, with no attempt to gain legal ownership.
flandrensis.pop: Nobody on the land; 741 online citizens in 2021
flandrensis.laws: A constitution; yearly elections until 2014; a Belgian non-profit since 2021

talossa-antarctic-claim.story: The Kingdom of Talossa is a self-declared country, or micronation, that began as a teenager's project in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and that also claims a part of Antarctica. Robert Ben Madison, aged 14, founded it in his bedroom on 26 December 1979, shortly after his mother died. He took the name after finding that it means inside the house in Finnish. Through his teens he produced a handwritten newspaper, a flag and an emblem, with about a dozen relatives and friends as members. In 1980 he began inventing a Talossan language, which now claims 35,000 root words. Talossa has had a website since 1995, and that web presence helped inspire later internet micronations. Its claim covers the east side of Milwaukee, the small French island of Cezembre and part of Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica. Its members live elsewhere and none on the Antarctic land. In 2000 Wired described it as one of the projects that claim territory but would not take power if offered it. On 5 August 2023 it counted 157 active citizens and 564 registered people in all. No state or United Nations body recognises any of the territory claimed.
talossa-antarctic-claim.mechanism: The Antarctic Treaty bars new claims on the continent, so a hobby state's claim there has no legal effect. Nobody is likely to inspect or contest it either.
talossa-antarctic-claim.laws: Its best-known creation is an invented language with a claimed 35,000 root words

westarctica.story: The Grand Duchy of Westarctica is a self-declared country, or micronation, claiming Marie Byrd Land, about 1.6 million square kilometres of West Antarctica and the one large area no country claims. In 2001 Travis McHenry, a United States Navy intelligence specialist, read in the CIA World Factbook that no state had claimed it, and he declared the Protectorate of Westarctica. He wrote letters to many countries, but only other micronations responded with recognition. In 2004 he began issuing fantasy passports as souvenirs, and he stopped after learning that a scammer in Kenya was selling them to refugees as real travel documents. By 2006 his Navy superiors knew he was writing to foreign governments and told him to choose. He kept his job and gave the title of Grand Duke to a friend, Philip Karns. He took the title back in 2010, and in 2014 he registered Westarctica as a non-profit that campaigns on climate. In July 2025 Indian police arrested Harsh Vardhan Jain for running a fake Westarctica embassy from a rented house in Ghaziabad. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty forbids any new claim while the treaty is in force, so the claim has no legal standing. Westarctica continues as an online project with no one on the land.
westarctica.mechanism: Even the one large unclaimed part of Antarctica cannot be claimed, because the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims. Documents issued for a private claim can still be misused by others as if they were real.
westarctica.passports: Fantasy passports from 2004, stopped after a Kenyan scammer sold them to refugees as real
westarctica.laws: Titles of nobility; a registered American non-profit since 2014

luxembourg-space-resources-2017.story: This is a law Luxembourg passed on 20 July 2017 saying companies can own materials they mine in space, the first such law in Europe. The small country had announced a programme called SpaceResources.lu in 2016 to attract space mining businesses, and at the time only the United States had a similar law. Article 1 says that space resources are capable of being owned, and the rest of the law sets out how missions are authorised and supervised. The difficulty is Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, which bars countries from claiming the Moon or other bodies in space. It binds Luxembourg, and Luxembourg's own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows a country to grant property rights in materials mined in space. The law tries to avoid the conflict by covering only the materials and saying nothing about ownership of the Moon or an asteroid. The two best-known asteroid mining firms of that period, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were both sold by January 2019. No court has tested the law.
luxembourg-space-resources-2017.mechanism: A small country can offer space miners a legal home by licensing them, and companies can then choose whichever country's law suits them best. The law covers mined materials and avoids any claim to land in space.
luxembourg-space-resources-2017.laws: Article 1 says space resources can be owned; missions need government approval
luxembourg-space-resources-2017.challenge: Doubted by Luxembourg's own Council of State; not tested in court

set.anchor: Luxembourg City. The law has no location in space.

luxembourg-space-resources-2017.why: Anchor text reworded to remove internal shorthand.

nemitz-eros.story: Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Carson City, Nevada, claimed in March 2000 to own Eros, an asteroid orbiting the Sun. He wanted to establish that private people can own property in space. His chance came on 12 February 2001, when NASA, the American space agency, landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe on Eros and left it there. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. NASA refused to pay, saying his claim had no basis in law. He then wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view private ownership of an asteroid is ruled out by Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space. On 3 November 2003 Nemitz filed a complaint in federal court in Reno, asking it to decide whether the treaty rules out private ownership of asteroids. The judge, Howard McKibben, ordered the case dismissed in April 2004. Nemitz appealed in July to the Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court in San Francisco, and the claim was dismissed in 2005. Press and bloggers called this the first legal case on property in space. Its main result was an official American government position against private ownership of an asteroid.
nemitz-eros.mechanism: The American State Department said Article II of the Outer Space Treaty rules out private ownership of an asteroid, and the courts refused to give Nemitz ownership.
nemitz-eros.stopped_by: NASA, the State Department and American federal courts
nemitz-eros.laws: A request to an American court to declare his rights
nemitz-eros.challenge: Lost. The case was dismissed in 2004 and the claim again in 2005 after appeal

set.anchor: Carson City, Nevada, Nemitz's home; the case began in federal court in Reno.

nemitz-eros.why: Anchor text reworded to remove internal shorthand.

planetary-resources-dsi.story: Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries were two companies, announced in the early 2010s, that planned to mine asteroids. Their plans helped push governments to write laws on who owns what is mined in space. Planetary Resources announced itself in 2012 with prominent business backers, and nine months later Deep Space Industries, founded by entrepreneurs and space advocates, announced similar plans to find and extract materials such as water ice. Both built small spacecraft, and both stood to gain when the United States passed its 2015 law and Luxembourg its 2017 one. Their money ran out before any mining began. In 2017 a funding round for Planetary Resources with a major mining company fell through, which led to large layoffs. In October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms and named only two of its people as staying. On 1 January 2019 Bradford Space announced that it had bought Deep Space Industries, whose work by then was on small-satellite engines. Jeff Foust, writing in The Space Review, concluded that the asteroid mining boom had been a bubble. The laws they helped inspire remain in force after both firms were sold.
planetary-resources-dsi.mechanism: National laws written with these firms in mind have outlasted them. The laws on owning mined space materials came before any actual mining took place.
planetary-resources-dsi.stopped_by: Lack of funding; bought by ConsenSys in October 2018 and Bradford Space in January 2019
planetary-resources-dsi.laws: Stood to benefit from American and Luxembourg laws on space resources

set.anchor: San Jose, California, base of Deep Space Industries.

planetary-resources-dsi.why: Anchor text reworded to remove internal shorthand.

uae-japan-space-resources.story: These are laws from the United Arab Emirates and Japan that allow companies to use materials mined in space, following the United States and Luxembourg. The Emirates' Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 covers licensing, registering spacecraft, liability and insurance, along with rules on building facilities on other planets and on using space resources. It had come into force by early 2020. Japan's parliament then passed Act No. 83 of 2021, on business activities in exploring and developing space resources, which made Japan the fourth country to pass such a law. Article 5 is headed Acquisition of Ownership of Space Resources, and according to the news site Atalayar the law lets Japanese companies find, extract and own minerals from the surface and subsurface of the Moon, Mars or other bodies. Japan's Hayabusa 2 mission had returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020, which showed that extraction is possible on a small scale. Together with the American and Luxembourg laws, these acts form a growing group of countries treating mining as a lawful use of space. No international treaty authorises this, and no court has tested the laws.
uae-japan-space-resources.mechanism: When several countries pass similar laws, their shared practice can start to shape international law. These countries are building that practice for ownership of mined space materials without any treaty authorising it.
uae-japan-space-resources.laws: Emirates Federal Law No. 12 of 2019; Japan's Act No. 83 of 2021, whose Article 5 covers ownership

set.anchor: Tokyo, Japan; the Emirates law comes from Abu Dhabi.

uae-japan-space-resources.why: Anchor text reworded to remove internal shorthand.

us-space-act-2015.story: This is an American law, signed on 25 November 2015, that gives American companies ownership of materials they mine in space. It is Title IV of the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act. Section 51303 of Title 51 of the United States Code says an American citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid or space resource is entitled to own, transport, use and sell it, as long as this complies with American law and international obligations. The wording tries to avoid a conflict with Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, which says outer space and bodies in it cannot be claimed by any nation. Opinio Juris, a law blog, wrote that Congress did this by giving the right to private citizens and not the nation, by making it subject to international obligations, and by disclaiming any sovereignty, meaning national ownership, over a body in space. A company could therefore own a tonne of mined ore while nobody owned the asteroid. Luxembourg copied the idea in 2017, and others followed. Whether one country can grant rights that others must respect is still debated, and no court ruling on the question has been reported.
us-space-act-2015.mechanism: American law grants ownership of mined materials while disclaiming any national ownership of the asteroid or moon they came from. This set the model of rights to the resources without rights to the land.
us-space-act-2015.laws: 51 USC 51303 says American citizens own the space resources they recover
us-space-act-2015.challenge: Debated by scholars; no court ruling reported

set.anchor: Washington, DC, seat of the American Congress.

us-space-act-2015.why: Anchor text reworded to remove internal shorthand.

chernobyl-samosely.story: The samosely, meaning self-settlers, are people who live inside the 30-kilometre Chernobyl Exclusion Zone in Ukraine and Belarus, the area emptied after the 1986 nuclear disaster, without official approval. Some refused to leave and others slipped back after the area was sealed off. About 1,200 people returned in 1986, out of about 100,000 evacuated. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster, and many had been told they could go home in a few days and then faced discrimination in the areas where they were resettled. Some outsiders came too. Ukraine's government has not legalised their settlements, because living in the zone remains prohibited, though a minister said in 2013 that they receive full social support and local officials have unofficially let elderly settlers stay. Numbers have fallen mainly through old age, from 314 in a 2007 census to 135 in 2017. Russian forces occupied the area in 2022, and residents have described that time as frightening. A Ukrainian report in April 2026 put the number left at about 25. None of them has declared a separate state, and they remain residents of the countries that run the zone.
chernobyl-samosely.mechanism: A government's evacuation order may go unenforced in practice, but people who stay gain no separate legal standing and remain under that government's law.
chernobyl-samosely.pop: About 1,200 returned in 1986; 135 in 2017; about 25 in 2026

add_sources.t: Chornobyl on hold: 40 years without solutions and with new threats, Frontliner, 24 Apr 2026
The main thing is that I am on my land, Real Gazeta

chernobyl-samosely.why: Population brought up to date: about 25 in April 2026 (Frontliner); the entry stopped at 135 in 2017.

cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.story: The United Nations Buffer Zone, also called the Green Line, is a strip of land patrolled by peacekeepers that runs 180 kilometres across the Mediterranean island of Cyprus and covers 346 square kilometres. It began in 1964 and was extended after the ceasefire of 16 August 1974, which followed the Turkish invasion and split the island between the Republic of Cyprus and the largely unrecognised Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. The strip ranges from under 20 metres to over 7 kilometres wide and cuts through the centre of the capital, Nicosia. About 10,000 people still live and farm in villages inside it, including Deneia, Athienou and Troulloi. Pyla is known as one of the few villages left in Cyprus where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. Crossing was very limited until April 2003, when the Turkish Cypriot administration eased its restrictions after nearly 30 years. No one has been reported trying to declare a separate state in the zone, and it remains under United Nations patrol.
cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.mechanism: A strip of land patrolled by peacekeepers does not end the claims of the states on either side, so people living inside it stay part of an existing state.
cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.laws: Patrolled by the United Nations force in Cyprus
cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.recognition: A ceasefire line run by the United Nations

korean-dmz-villages.story: The Korean Demilitarized Zone is a strip about 250 kilometres long and 4 kilometres wide separating North and South Korea, and two villages are allowed to remain inside it. It was created by the armistice, or ceasefire agreement, of 27 July 1953, when each side moved its troops back 2,000 metres from the front. Its edges are among the most heavily armed borders in the world. Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side and is governed and protected by the United Nations Command. Its residents, 218 people in 2008, descend from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens but do not pay tax or do military service. Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side, with brightly painted concrete buildings. Only North Korea or the United Nations Command can give access, and both villages remain in place under the armistice.
korean-dmz-villages.mechanism: Living inside an armistice zone depends on permission from the bodies that run the ceasefire, and residents keep the citizenship of a country on one side.
korean-dmz-villages.laws: Armistice rules, applied by the United Nations Command in the south

greenland-purchase-offers.story: The United States has tried several times to buy Greenland, the Arctic island that belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark and governs itself. Secretary of State William Seward backed a purchase in 1867, the same year the country bought Alaska, and there were talks again in 1910. In 1946 the United States secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold, which Denmark rejected. In 2019 President Trump said he wanted to buy the island, and Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen called the idea absurd and said Greenland was not for sale. In his second term from 2025 Trump pressed again and spoke of tariffs against Denmark. In January 2026 Greenland's leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said Greenland would choose Denmark, and reports put opposition to an American takeover at 85 percent of Greenlanders. Under Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum. On 22 September 2026 the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement in New York with no expiry date. It expands the American military presence and bars countries outside NATO, the Western military alliance, from setting up military installations. Frederiksen said it recognises Denmark's sovereignty, meaning its legal ownership, and the Greenlandic people's right to decide their own future. No sale has taken place.
greenland-purchase-offers.mechanism: Territory cannot be bought without the seller's consent, and in Greenland's case the law puts the decision on independence with the local people.
greenland-purchase-offers.challenge: The Danish and Greenlandic governments rejected each offer
greenland-purchase-offers.recognition: None sought; Greenland remains part of the Kingdom of Denmark

romanov-empire-bakov.story: The Romanov Empire is a self-declared country, or micronation, with no land of its own, started in 2011 by Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman and former member of the Russian parliament. He says it restores the Russian Empire. In 2014 it issued a manifesto naming the German prince Karl Emich of Leiningen as Emperor Nicholas III, and in 2017 it took the name Romanov Empire. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about $31, and claimed to have issued about 4,000 by 2014. To become a real state it needed territory, so Bakov talked with several countries about buying land. As of 2017, talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Nicholas III also wrote to Vladimir Putin asking for land in Yekaterinburg for a capital, and that request was denied. In July 2013 Bakov said his state had granted citizenship to Edward Snowden, who was then staying in Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow. In 2020 Bakov said a successor project called Arca Noë would be based on a floating settlement in neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. No report says it was built.
romanov-empire-bakov.mechanism: A private buyer needs a government willing to give up part of its territory, and the governments approached did not agree.
romanov-empire-bakov.stopped_by: Talks to buy land from governments failed

state-to-state-purchases.story: Countries have sold land to each other for centuries, and a Wikipedia list records the deals in which money was paid for sovereignty, meaning legal ownership by a state. Scotland paid Norway 4,000 marks sterling for the Isle of Man and the Hebrides in 1266. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about $7 per square kilometre, and paid Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about $4 per square kilometre. It paid Denmark $25 million for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies in 1916, or $62,500 per square kilometre. As part of that deal it recognised Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland, a promise that came up again in later offers to buy the island. Brazil paid Bolivia £2 million for Acre in 1903. The last sale on the list is Gwadar, which Pakistan bought from Muscat and Oman for £3 million in 1958. Every buyer and seller on the list is a state or a ruler, and the list leaves out leases and payments for other purposes such as war damages. No private buyer appears on it.
state-to-state-purchases.mechanism: A state can sell land by treaty, and every sale on this list was made between states or rulers.
state-to-state-purchases.recognition: Each sale was a treaty between the two parties

arctic-sanctuary-greenpeace-flag.story: The Arctic sanctuary is a campaign by the environmental group Greenpeace to protect the waters around the North Pole, which lie beyond the national zones of the countries bordering the Arctic Ocean. Greenpeace wants the area kept free of oil drilling and mining. In April 2013 four young people working with the group, led by two young Indigenous Arctic people, trekked to the Pole and cut a hole in the ice. They lowered a flag designed by a child from Malaysia to the seabed about four kilometres down, where Russia had placed its own flag in 2007. The flag was attached to a glass and titanium capsule holding the signatures of nearly three million people asking for a global sanctuary. Governments have discussed the idea too. In 2008 the European Parliament suggested a treaty modelled on the Antarctic Treaty for the unpopulated and unclaimed centre of the Arctic Ocean, and in a 2014 resolution it called for a sanctuary in the waters outside coastal states' zones. No such sanctuary has been created, and the proposal remains a campaign aim.
arctic-sanctuary-greenpeace-flag.mechanism: Nobody owns these waters, so no single country can make them a sanctuary. Protection depends on countries agreeing a new treaty.
arctic-sanctuary-greenpeace-flag.recognition: The European Parliament called for a sanctuary; none has become law

arktika-2007-flag.story: In August 2007 a Russian expedition sent two small Mir submarines to the seabed at the North Pole and planted a rust-proof titanium flag there, at a depth of 4,261 metres. Its leader was Artur Chilingarov, a member of parliament, and a research ship carried about 100 scientists. Russia wanted to support its case that part of the Arctic seabed belongs to it, a case it had first submitted in 2001, and Chilingarov said people could find the flag in a thousand years. Canada's foreign minister Peter MacKay answered that this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory. A State Department spokesman in the United States said the flag had no legal standing. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre explained that the 200-nautical-mile zones of the five Arctic coastal states leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres in question. Any country wanting that seabed has to build a scientific case under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a process separate from flag-planting. He called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim. The flag remains a symbol with no legal effect.
arktika-2007-flag.mechanism: Planting a flag gives no ownership of the deep seabed. A country can extend its seabed rights only by presenting scientific evidence under the Law of the Sea treaty.
arktika-2007-flag.laws: Open ocean beyond national zones; the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea sets the process for seabed claims
arktika-2007-flag.challenge: Canada and the United States rejected it as a legal act

eastern-greenland-case.story: This was a 1931 attempt by Norway to take a stretch of Greenland's east coast from Denmark, which ended in a defeat at the world court of the time. The area was uninhabited apart from three main Norwegian stations. In June 1931 Hallvard Devold, a founder of the Norwegian Arctic Trading Company, raised the Norwegian flag at one of them, Myggbukta. On 10 July Norway issued a royal proclamation occupying the area and named it Erik the Red's Land. Norway argued that this part of Greenland was terra nullius, land belonging to no state, because Denmark had never effectively occupied it. Denmark went to the Permanent Court of International Justice two days later and asked it to declare the occupation unlawful and invalid. The case also turned on the Ihlen Declaration, in which Norway's foreign minister told the Danish minister in July 1919 that Norway would not make difficulties over Denmark's claim to all of Greenland. On 5 April 1933 the court ruled for Denmark by twelve votes to two and found the proclamation unlawful and invalid. Norway then gave up the claim.
eastern-greenland-case.mechanism: Light use of remote land can still be enough for a state to own it, if that state has shown authority there. A later proclamation and a few private stations did not displace Denmark.
eastern-greenland-case.recognition: None; the court ruled the occupation invalid

hans-island.story: Hans Island, called Tartupaluk in Greenlandic, is a bare rock of 1.3 square kilometres in Nares Strait, between Canada's Ellesmere Island and Greenland, which Canada and Denmark both claimed for decades. In 1973 the two countries agreed a sea boundary through the strait but could not agree who owned the island. Denmark pointed to an expedition with Danish participation that named the island in 1853, and to its geology and slightly closer position to Greenland. Canada said Denmark's claim had lapsed. NPR reported a summer of flag-planting and gift-leaving in 2005, when Denmark sent a warship after Canada's defence minister raised a flag there. On 14 June 2022 the foreign ministers Melanie Joly of Canada and Jeppe Kofod of Denmark and Greenland's premier Mute Egede settled it and exchanged bottles of Canadian whisky and Danish bitter. The agreement split the island along a natural ridge, roughly 60 percent to Denmark and the rest to Canada, which gave the two countries their first land border. It also settled their remaining sea boundary in the Lincoln and Labrador seas.
hans-island.mechanism: Two countries disputing an uninhabited rock can divide it by agreement, without going to court over who owns it.
hans-island.stopped_by: Settled by Canada, Denmark and Greenland on 14 June 2022
hans-island.why: Legal point said the island was divided in half; the agreement gives roughly 60 percent to Denmark, as the story states.

svalbard-treaty.story: The Svalbard Treaty gave Norway a group of Arctic islands, about twice the size of Belgium, on condition that citizens of other treaty countries can live and do business there. Until the 20th century Svalbard was terra nullius, meaning land belonging to no state. Whalers and then miners from many countries worked there with almost no law, and disputes between miners and owners created demand for a government. The treaty, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920, recognised Norway's full and unqualified sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, and came into force on 14 August 1925. In exchange Norway accepted limits. Citizens and companies of every treaty country may live there and have equal rights to fish, hunt, mine and run businesses. Norway may tax only enough to pay for running Svalbard, so its budget is kept apart from the mainland's. Article 9 bans naval bases and fortifications, and no visa is needed to enter. Russia uses its rights through its settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden. The treaty began with 14 parties and had 49 by 2026. About 2,500 people live on the islands, and Norway still governs them under the treaty.
svalbard-treaty.mechanism: Unowned land can be handed to one country by treaty while other countries keep guaranteed rights to work there. Svalbard has run this way under a single government for a century.
svalbard-treaty.laws: Norwegian rule with limits set by the treaty; a separate budget and limited taxes
svalbard-treaty.challenge: Stable since 1925; Russia keeps settlements there under its treaty rights
svalbard-treaty.passports: No visa needed to enter, under the treaty

t3-ice-island-escamilla.story: T-3 was a drifting iceberg in the Arctic Ocean, about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as a staffed American research station from 1952 to 1978, with huts, a power plant and an airstrip. It became a legal puzzle after a killing. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla, a member of the station team armed with a borrowed rifle during a dispute over raisin wine, shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey. The island was then inside the Arctic sector Canada had claimed, but Canada chose not to act. American officials flew Escamilla to Dulles Airport in Virginia and charged him, arguing that the ice was on the high seas, the open ocean outside every country's waters, and so within the special American law for crimes at sea. A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter and he received three years. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law covered an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place. It overturned the conviction for other trial errors and ordered a new trial, at which he was acquitted. Congress did not settle the question of jurisdiction, meaning legal authority over such a place, until a change to federal law in 1984.
t3-ice-island-escamilla.mechanism: An unclaimed moving ice island is not clearly land or a ship. The evenly split court left open whether a country's law could reach it, until Congress legislated.
t3-ice-island-escamilla.laws: American federal law was applied; the only authority on site was a station manager
t3-ice-island-escamilla.challenge: The American court kept the case, because the appeal judges split evenly
t3-ice-island-escamilla.stopped_by: The station was abandoned and the ice drifted on

wrangel-island-expedition.story: Wrangel Island lies in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia, and in 1921 the Arctic explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson tried to claim it by placing settlers there. Survivors of the crushed ship Karluk, from an expedition he organised, had been stranded on it for nine months in 1914. In 1921 he sent five people: Allan Crawford of Canada, the Americans Fred Maurer, Lorne Knight and Milton Galle, and Ada Blackjack, an Iñupiat seamstress and cook. The aim was to claim the island for Canada, and Stefansson said he wanted to head off a Japanese claim, although Russia had declared the island its own in 1916. A relief ship failed to get through the ice in 1922. In January 1923 Crawford, Maurer and Galle set out across the frozen sea to Siberia for help and were never seen again. Knight died of scurvy that June. Blackjack, left alone, survived until a ship rescued her in August. That ship left a new party of 13, the American Charles Wells and 12 Inuit. In 1924 the Soviet Union sent the ship Krasny Oktyabr, or Red October, and removed them, by then 14 people after a birth. Wells died of pneumonia in Vladivostok, two children died, and the survivors got home with money raised by the American Red Cross. The island remains Russian and became a World Heritage Site in 2004.
wrangel-island-expedition.mechanism: The nearest state can remove a small private colony on remote land with a single ship. Occupying a place gives no protection without a government's backing.
wrangel-island-expedition.pop: Five settlers in 1921; 13 people left there in 1923
wrangel-island-expedition.challenge: Failed; a Soviet ship removed the settlers

deepsea-ventures-claim.story: In 1974 an American company, Deepsea Ventures Inc. of Gloucester Point, Virginia, claimed the sole right to mine a patch of the northeastern Pacific seabed that lay outside every country's control. The target was manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps of metal on the ocean floor, in a deposit covering 60,000 square kilometres. At the time no treaty said who could mine the deep seabed, because the Law of the Sea treaty was still being negotiated. On 15 November the company's president, John Flipse, sent a notice of discovery to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, asking the American government for diplomatic protection, and recorded a copy at a local courthouse. Copies went to cabinet members, congressional committees, ambassadors of maritime countries, oceanographers and other companies. The magazine Reason called it the world's first ocean mining claim. The company promised commercial production within 15 years, running for 40 years. It asserted exclusive rights to mine and sell the nodules, and said it was claiming no territory and was not asking the United States to do so. The 1982 treaty later put the area under an international authority. No report says that mining took place under the claim or that a court ever ruled on it.
deepsea-ventures-claim.mechanism: Deepsea Ventures tried to create private rights to seabed minerals by discovering them and giving public notice, without claiming the seabed itself. The Law of the Sea treaty later gave the area to an international authority.
deepsea-ventures-claim.challenge: Filed as a private claim; no court ruling is reported
deepsea-ventures-claim.cost: A tract of 60,000 square kilometres, with commercial production planned within 15 years

international-seabed-authority.story: The International Seabed Authority is an international body based in Kingston, Jamaica, that controls mining on the ocean floor outside any country's control, an area covering about half of the world's oceans. It was set up on 16 November 1994 under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and has 172 members, made up of 171 countries and the European Union. No person or country can own that seabed by claiming it, so a company wanting to mine there needs a contract with the authority and the backing of a member country, called a sponsor. Since 1994 the authority has approved more than two dozen exploration contracts in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, most in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico. It has not approved any commercial mining. Its council met in March 2026 without finishing its long-delayed mining rules, with benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. The authority also opened an inquiry into whether two contractors, NORI and TOML, had broken their obligations by seeking American mining permits. On 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal ordered it to respect due process, meaning fair procedure, in that inquiry. Two days later the council extended NORI's exploration contract to 2031. The United States has not ratified the treaty and is not a member.
international-seabed-authority.mechanism: The deep seabed is run by an international body, so a company needs a contract with the authority and a sponsoring country. Finding minerals or occupying a spot gives no right to them.
international-seabed-authority.laws: Rules for commercial mining were still unfinished in 2026
international-seabed-authority.challenge: In force; the United States is not a member and has opened its own permit route
international-seabed-authority.recognition: 172 members: 171 countries and the European Union

metals-company.story: The Metals Company is a business that wants to mine metal-rich nodules from the Pacific seabed, and it is testing whether it can do so with an American permit outside the international system. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011. The International Seabed Authority, the body that controls the deep ocean floor, granted exploration contracts in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, about 1,500 miles southwest of San Diego, to two companies backed by small Pacific states: NORI, sponsored by Nauru, and TOML, sponsored by Tonga. DeepGreen owned NORI and later bought TOML, and in 2021 it went public under its current name. That June, Nauru told the authority it meant to begin mining, which started a two-year deadline to finish the rules. The rules were not finished. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the American ocean agency, to speed up permits under an American law on seabed mining, and four days later the company's American arm applied. NOAA published its application for public comment in August 2026, and no permit had been issued by that month. The authority opened an inquiry into NORI and TOML, and the two companies took it to a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal in June 2026. On 18 July the chamber ordered the authority to respect fair procedure in the inquiry, without suspending it. The main case is undecided. NORI's contract was extended to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending.
metals-company.mechanism: The company is testing whether a firm can mine the international seabed under one country's permit, while its own subsidiaries hold contracts under the treaty system that the permit would bypass.
metals-company.challenge: The companies are suing the Seabed Authority over its inquiry, and the tribunal ordered fair procedure on 18 July 2026 with the main case pending; no American permit had been issued as of August 2026
metals-company.recognition: Seabed Authority contracts through Nauru and Tonga; applications under American law
metals-company.cost: DeepGreen merged with a listed shell company, a firm with a stock listing and no business, in a $2.9 billion deal in 2021

afropolitan.story: Afropolitan is a company in the San Francisco Bay Area that has marketed itself as a digital nation for the African diaspora. It began in 2016 as a networking and events business for wealthy members of the diaspora. In May 2022, its founders Eche Emole and Chika Uwazie announced a four-part plan for what the tech news site Built In reported as the world's first digital nation, aimed at fostering the Black community. They drew on the network-state idea of the entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan, who argues that online communities can grow into countries. They compared it to Facebook as a country, with its own laws, currency and culture. The company raised $2.1 million in seed funding, money from early investors, and in September 2022 Uwazie rang the closing bell at the New York Stock Exchange. A critical 2025 article on the website Africa Is a Country found that three years on, the founders ran a podcast and three services launched in late 2024, namely a dating service, paid mentoring and an event-booking app. The writer said the digital nation idea served as a hook for investors. No report describes any territory, passport or legal status, and Afropolitan continues as a company.
afropolitan.mechanism: Calling a networking company a nation creates no legal status. It remains a company under the law of the country where it is registered.

barbados-metaverse-embassy.story: This is a plan by the Caribbean country of Barbados to open an embassy in the metaverse, meaning online 3D worlds where people move around as animated figures. On 14 November 2021 its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade signed an agreement with Decentraland, a virtual world with over 90,000 plots of land bought with cryptocurrency. Talks with two other platforms, Somnium Space and SuperWorld, were being finalised. Gabriel Abed, a crypto entrepreneur and Barbados's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, brokered the deal. The embassy would offer services such as electronic visas, and the country planned to declare its virtual land sovereign, meaning under its own authority. Avinash Persaud, special envoy to Prime Minister Mia Mottley, called it the first official embassy or lookout post in the metaverse and promised a report in twelve months. A CoinDesk opinion piece called the idea a gimmick and asked why a website would not do. An opening was first expected around January 2022, and in February a newsletter still described it as coming soon. An article from June 2022 said it was tentatively scheduled for later that month. No report confirms that the embassy opened or that the promised report appeared.
barbados-metaverse-embassy.mechanism: A government declaring virtual land to be sovereign changes nothing under the law of diplomacy unless other countries accept it, and no other country is reported to have done so.
barbados-metaverse-embassy.recognition: Barbados itself only; no other country is reported to accept it

add_sources.t: Barbados opens the world's first recognised sovereign embassy in the metaverse, Fanatical Futurist, 14 Jun 2022
Not much seems to have happened, Links I Would Gchat You, 11 Feb 2022

barlow-declaration.story: A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace is a short manifesto claiming that governments have no authority over the internet. John Perry Barlow, a founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a group that campaigns for rights online, published it on the web on 8 February 1996 from Davos, Switzerland. He wrote it for a project called 24 Hours in Cyberspace. It addressed the governments of the industrial world as weary giants of flesh and steel and told them they had no sovereignty, meaning legal authority, where its authors gathered. In sixteen short paragraphs it argued that the United States lacked the consent of the governed to apply its laws to the internet, and that the internet lay outside every country's borders. The document created no institutions, members, courts or money. Governments have since acted against its claim, because the physical parts of a network, such as servers, satellites and ground stations, and the people who run them, sit where governments can reach them. The text is still online at the Electronic Frontier Foundation.
barlow-declaration.mechanism: The text argued that authority online should rest on the consent of users and not on geography. No government has accepted this.

bitnation.story: Bitnation was an online project that called itself a voluntary nation, with records of identity, marriage, birth and contracts kept on a blockchain, a shared public ledger, in place of government registers. Susanne Tarkowski Tempelhof founded it in July 2014, and people chose to join. In 2015 it launched software for blockchain ID cards and offered Bitcoin debit cards to refugees reaching Europe. From December 2015 it offered a blockchain notary service to e-residents of Estonia, foreigners who hold a digital identity from that country. Tempelhof told IBTimes she hoped Bitnation would be recognised as a sovereign entity, which would set a precedent for a piece of open software counting as a jurisdiction, meaning an area of legal authority. In 2017 it launched Pangea, a system for settling disputes by private arbitration, with its own token, and its refugee ID won a UNESCO prize. A Vice writer who joined in 2016 found about 25 volunteer embassies, including a German castle run as a bed and breakfast, and reported limited services and little interest. Because no state recognised Bitnation, it had no legal authority, and an embassy could do little for an asylum seeker. By August 2022 its web domain had been sold and the project was considered defunct.
bitnation.mechanism: A blockchain can record a marriage or an ID, but those records carry legal weight only where a recognised state chooses to accept them.
bitnation.stopped_by: It faded; its web domain had been sold by August 2022
bitnation.currency: A token for its Pangea dispute system was proposed
bitnation.passports: Blockchain ID cards for refugees, which no state recognises
bitnation.laws: Records kept on a blockchain; disputes settled by private arbitration through Pangea
bitnation.challenge: Vice reported it has no legal authority, since no state recognises it

citydao.story: CityDAO is an online group that bought 40 acres of rural Wyoming, in the United States, with the stated aim of building a city of the future with all its records on a blockchain, a shared public ledger. A DAO, or decentralised autonomous organisation, is a group that makes decisions and holds money through software on a blockchain. Scott Fitsimones started the idea with a tweet in July 2021, just after Wyoming's new DAO law took effect, because Wyoming was then the only state letting such a group hold property as a company. In October 2021 the group bought the land, called Parcel 0, west of Clark and about 30 minutes from Cody, for around $100,000. Members hold a digital token called a Citizenship NFT and vote on proposals. In June 2022 CityDAO told a Wyoming legislative committee it had about 6,500 citizens and floated the idea of incorporating an actual city, if counties agreed, with deeds, titles and tax records on the blockchain. It has never claimed independence, and citizen here only means someone who holds the token. In May 2023 the local press reported that the land was undeveloped, with a well and a flat building area, and that zoning rules may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot. No later report says what has become of the project.
citydao.mechanism: A blockchain community can own land through a company chartered by a state, and every member stays subject to that state's ordinary law.
citydao.pop: No residents reported; about 6,500 token-holding citizens in June 2022
citydao.currency: None; the Citizenship NFT is a membership token
citydao.passports: A Citizenship NFT, which gives no legal citizenship
citydao.challenge: Not challenged; it is a company under Wyoming law
citydao.recognition: Recognised only as a Wyoming company

add_sources.t: Wyoming's First Digital Land Buy Was CityDAO, Cowboy State Daily, 14 May 2023

decentraland-land.story: Decentraland is an online 3D world where people buy plots of virtual land, created by the Argentine developers Ari Meilich and Esteban Ordano beginning in 2015. It raised $26 million by selling digital coins in 2017 and opened to the public in February 2020. Land is sold as tokens, digital ownership records on the Ethereum blockchain, and paid for with the world's own currency, MANA. Its first map, Genesis City, has 90,601 plots, sold at about $20 each at launch. During the cryptocurrency boom prices reached $6,000 to $100,000 in April 2021, and a company paid $2.43 million for a plot that November. Users govern the world through a community vote and a nonprofit foundation, and a November 2021 vote on banning the name Hitler failed to reach enough votes to take effect.
