Use stayed small, and the analytics firm DappRadar counted fewer than 1,000 users a day making transactions in October 2022. Decentraland remains open to users today.
decentraland-land.mechanism: Owning a token gives a right inside one platform's rules. It gives no land under any country's law.
decentraland-land.cost: The highest reported plot sale was $2.43 million, in November 2021

set.anchor: Buenos Aires, placed for the founders' Argentine origin.

decentraland-land.why: Anchor text reworded to remove research narration.

dominion-of-melchizedek.story: The Dominion of Melchizedek is a self-declared country, regarded by American regulators as non-existent, that has been used to sell passports, bank licences and financial paper. The American Mark Pedley declared it in 1990, possibly with his father David, who had been convicted of financial crimes in the 1970s. Mark had his own convictions, including a $6 million currency fraud in 1986, and his parole was revoked in 1991 for promoting a fictitious country. Melchizedek had no fixed home. It claimed Malpelo, a Colombian island, then Karitane Shoal in the South Pacific, a place that appears to have been invented and that its spokesman described as 14 square miles of sandy beaches. It also claimed French-owned Clipperton Island, Bokak Atoll in the Marshall Islands and part of Antarctica. About 300 bank licences were claimed to have been sold by the end of the 1990s, and in 1991 shell banks in Washington, D.C., tried to get loans with fake Melchizedek securities and were shut down. One investment scheme took over $4 million from at least 1,400 people. Passports sold for up to $3,500, and three people posing as officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998. That April the Marshall Islands government condemned its claims as fraudulent. One source puts the total raised above $500 million. Pedley pleaded guilty to share manipulation in 2010, and his wife Pearlasia Gamboa, Melchizedek's president, lost a $1.8 million civil judgment that year. No report says it has been formally dissolved.
dominion-of-melchizedek.mechanism: A claim to sovereignty can be used to sell passports and financial paper, with claims to reefs and shoals and no one living there. Ordinary fraud law applies to the people selling them.
dominion-of-melchizedek.stopped_by: The Marshall Islands condemned it, and people tied to it were convicted of crimes
dominion-of-melchizedek.passports: Sold widely and regarded as fraudulent; a 1998 Philippine scheme took in about $1 million
dominion-of-melchizedek.challenge: It held no territory to defend; people linked to it were convicted of fraud
dominion-of-melchizedek.recognition: The Central African Republic reportedly in 1993, per the Washington Post; otherwise none
dominion-of-melchizedek.cost: One source estimates over $500 million raised across its schemes

elgaland-vargaland.story: The Kingdoms of Elgaland-Vargaland is an art project in the form of a country, a self-declared state known as a micronation. The Swedish artists Carl Michael von Hauswolff and Leif Elggren announced it in a newspaper advertisement on 27 May 1992. Its founding constitution claims the places other countries leave out. Its physical territory is the border zones between all countries on Earth, plus sea areas up to 10 nautical miles wide outside every country's territorial waters. It also claims states of mind and unreal places, including the Hypnagogic State, the moment between waking and sleep, and a digital Virtual Room. It regards all dead people as citizens, and it reported 980 living citizens in 2014. The founders issue a flag, anthem, stamps and passports on request, and they hold exhibitions called embassies, including in Reykjavik in 1994, Berlin in 2006 and Morocco in 2014. They applied for United Nations membership in 1994. In 2002 a group travelling on its passports was detained in Estonia and sent back to Sweden the next day. No activity after 2014 is reported.
elgaland-vargaland.mechanism: As art, the project treats borders and virtual space as land that can be claimed. It shows how far a declaration can go when nobody has to respond to it.
elgaland-vargaland.laws: A founding constitution describing a divine monarchy
elgaland-vargaland.recognition: None; it is an art project

estonia-data-embassy.story: The Estonian Data Embassy is a set of government computer servers kept in a data centre in Luxembourg and treated much like an embassy. Estonia, a small Baltic country, runs much of its government online, and it wanted its state records to survive if its own territory was ever attacked or occupied. Work began in 2015, and in 2017 the two countries signed an agreement. Estonia's servers sit in a high-security data centre in Luxembourg and stay under Estonian control. Luxembourg's IT director Patrick Houtsch told NBC News that his government provided the data centre services along with immunity, meaning protection from local law. In June 2019 Estonia moved four core databases there, including land and business registries. The Estonian government calls it something new under international law, an extension of the state in the cloud. It draws on the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, the treaty that protects embassies, but it is not an embassy in the traditional sense. The arrangement starts from a recognised state, which gets immunity by agreement with another recognised state, and the registries could keep running if Estonia lost its land. Estonia's government still describes the arrangement as running.
estonia-data-embassy.mechanism: An agreement between two countries can give a state's core data immunity abroad. This separates some government functions from territory, but only with the host country's consent.
estonia-data-embassy.laws: An agreement between the two countries, drawing on the treaty that protects embassies
estonia-data-embassy.recognition: An agreement between two recognised states

estonia-e-residency.story: E-Residency is a programme run by the government of Estonia, a Baltic country, that gives foreigners a secure digital identity so they can set up and run Estonian companies online. Launched at the end of 2014, it lets people do this without ever visiting. It does not make anyone a citizen or give the right to live there. Here a real state hands out a digital status, the reverse of a micronation, a self-declared state with no real government behind it. The official dashboard says over 144,000 people from 187 countries have become e-residents and that they have founded or co-founded more than 44,000 Estonian companies. In 2025 they set up a record 5,556 companies, and the state received nearly €125 million in direct revenue, mainly from taxes on wages and on dividends. The economy minister said every euro invested brought more than 12 back. Figures reported in September 2026 show over 4,200 new companies and about 9,000 new e-residents so far that year. The system works without land of its own because it relies on Estonia's existing territory, law, courts and banks. The programme continues to take new applicants.
estonia-e-residency.mechanism: An existing country can offer legal identity and company law to people living elsewhere, online. This gives them much of what online nations promise, backed by a recognised state.
estonia-e-residency.passports: None; a digital ID without citizenship or the right to live there
estonia-e-residency.challenge: Not challenged; it is a government programme

liberland-metaverse.story: The Liberland Metaverse is a planned online 3D city for Liberland, a self-declared country on land between Serbia and Croatia. The Czech activist Vít Jedlička declared Liberland in 2015, and no state recognises it. Serbia's foreign ministry has called it a frivolous act needing no further comment. Croatia controls access to the land. In early 2022 the architecture firm Zaha Hadid Architects, under its principal Patrik Schumacher, released designs for the virtual city, with curving buildings, a City Hall, a plaza and an exhibition centre, hosted on a platform called Mytaverse. Buyers could purchase virtual land and set up businesses there, and they would also get a stake in the physical Liberland. Schumacher said the aim was to support Liberland's development as a libertarian micronation and to make a meeting place for cryptocurrency and online developers. He also argued that open virtual worlds run by their communities will beat those run by corporations. In November 2022 press reports still described Liberland as about to become a country in the metaverse. No report says how many plots were sold or whether the city is in use.
liberland-metaverse.mechanism: A virtual city gives a claimed state with no physical access a place to gather, but it changes nothing about the claim to the land.
liberland-metaverse.challenge: Croatia controls access to the land
liberland-metaverse.why: Added the start year, which was missing: Dezeen, Domus and Hypebeast coverage dates to March 2022.

add_sources.t: Zaha Hadid Architects designs virtual Liberland Metaverse city, Dezeen
Liberland becomes the first country to debut in the metaverse, Investing.com, 8 Nov 2022
Liberland is the first metaverse city designed by Zaha Hadid, Domus, 15 Mar 2022

nansen-passport.story: The Nansen passport was a travel document for people with no country, issued from 1922 under the League of Nations, the international body before the United Nations. In 1921 the Soviet government revoked the citizenship of Russians living abroad, including some 800,000 refugees from the civil war. These people could not cross a border legally, because no state would issue them papers. The League's High Commissioner for Refugees, the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, called a conference in Geneva in July 1922 that agreed a travel document for stateless people, which came to carry his name. It was extended to Armenian refugees in 1924 and to Assyrian, Bulgarian and Turkish ones in 1928. About 450,000 were issued. After Nansen died in 1930, the Nansen International Office for Refugees ran the system, and it won the 1938 Nobel Peace Prize, the year it closed. Later documents for refugees and stateless people come from national and international authorities. The passport worked because governments had agreed in advance to honour it, unlike Garry Davis's later World Passport. Holders still lived under the law of whichever state they had reached.
nansen-passport.mechanism: An identity document can work with no territory behind it when countries agree to honour it. Its authority comes from those countries.
nansen-passport.stopped_by: Replaced when the Nansen Office closed in 1938 and later refugee documents took over
nansen-passport.pop: About 450,000 holders, with no territory of their own
nansen-passport.challenge: Accepted by states; the office running it won the 1938 Nobel Peace Prize
nansen-passport.recognition: Recognised internationally through agreements among governments

network-state-school.story: The Network State is an idea for starting new countries online, and the Network School is its test site. Balaji Srinivasan, former chief technology officer of the cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase, set out the idea in a 2022 book. An online community forms first, buys land in scattered places with pooled money and eventually seeks diplomatic recognition from real governments. In August 2024 he announced the Network School in a hotel at Forest City, a half-empty development in Johor, Malaysia. It became permanent in May 2025, with fees of about $1,500 to $3,000 a month. After social media claims that Israelis had entered on second passports, Malaysian officers inspected the site on 14 July 2026. They checked 266 foreigners from 40 countries and found all documents valid. Commentators also objected to its stated aims on sovereignty, and Srinivasan suspended a planned $500 million investment. On 21 July the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked the school's business licence, citing breaches of licence conditions and of how the premises could be used, and ordered it to stop the next day. Within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum, a non-binding statement of intent, to host a campus. Network School Kazakhstan launched at a centre in Astana on 2 September 2026, with Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev taking part.
network-state-school.mechanism: A community that begins online still needs a host country for its physical base, and that country's ordinary licensing power can shut it down.
network-state-school.stopped_by: The Iskandar Puteri City Council in Malaysia, which revoked its licence on 21 July 2026
network-state-school.laws: Membership rules, under Malaysian licensing and immigration law while it was there
network-state-school.challenge: Lost its licence in Malaysia; moved to Astana, Kazakhstan, in September 2026 under a July memorandum
network-state-school.recognition: None; Kazakhstan's ministry signed a non-binding memorandum
network-state-school.cost: Fees of about $1,500 to $3,000 a month; Srinivasan said over $100 million was committed and suspended a further $500 million

order-of-malta.story: The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is a Catholic religious order that has no land but is treated as a sovereign body, like a state, in international law. It began in the 11th century as a hospital community in Jerusalem, and Pope Paschal II approved it in 1113. It later ruled the island of Rhodes and then Malta, which it defended for more than three months against the Ottoman Empire in the Great Siege of 1565. In June 1798 Napoleon's forces took Malta and the Order lost its last territory. Other countries went on treating it as a sovereign body. Its only property of this kind is two headquarters buildings in Rome with extraterritorial status, meaning Italian law treats them as outside normal Italian control. It issues its own passports, coins and stamps, and signs treaties. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, while Wikipedia gives 115 states. The United Nations General Assembly made it a permanent observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. Three principal officers count as citizens. It says its diplomatic network exists to give its medical programmes protected access in crisis regions.
order-of-malta.mechanism: Sovereignty in the sense of diplomatic recognition can survive the loss of all territory, if enough countries keep treating the body as a sovereign partner.
order-of-malta.pop: Three principal officers count as citizens; no one lives on a territory of its own
order-of-malta.laws: Its own constitution, a Grand Master and treaties with states
order-of-malta.challenge: Lost Malta to Napoleon in 1798 and kept its sovereign status
order-of-malta.recognition: Diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, by its own count; United Nations observer since 1994

pirate-party-hosting.story: In 2010 the Swedish Pirate Party, a small political party that campaigns against strict copyright law, became the internet provider for The Pirate Bay, a site for finding shared files. The party's founder Rick Falkvinge later wrote that this political step shielded it legally. The party then went further. In July 2010 it proposed that, if elected to the Swedish parliament on 19 September, it would host The Pirate Bay from inside the building. It argued that a rule protecting members of parliament would give total immunity, meaning protection from prosecution, for any political action in that workplace. The plan needed seats, and the party had none. It won 0.65 percent in the election and no seats, so the plan never took effect. The party also offered to host WikiLeaks and launched an anonymous internet provider. In 2013 Falkvinge wrote that The Pirate Bay's address still ended at the party's network, and the site later moved to many places, including encrypted cloud services.
pirate-party-hosting.mechanism: The Pirate Party tried to use the immunity of members of parliament in place of offshore distance, so a site's safe harbour would be built from a state's own law.
pirate-party-hosting.laws: Swedish parliamentary immunity was the proposed protection

praxis.story: Praxis is a New York company that has spent years trying to find a site for a new city run on its own terms. Dryden Brown, a former hedge fund analyst, and Charlie Callinan founded it in 2019. That year they went to Nigeria and Ghana and proposed a financial centre to Ghana's vice-president. The firm later described plans for a city of 10,000 people, first in the Mediterranean, then in Greenland, then in Uruguay. In 2024 Gizmodo, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported $525 million in new funding. Of this, $500 million was a drawdown facility from the crypto firm GEM Digital, meaning money released only once conditions are met, here listing Praxis tokens on a public exchange. Also in 2024 Brown wrote that he had flown to Nuuk to try to buy Greenland. He then told TechCrunch he hoped to work with the government on a new city on uninhabitable land. Danish MP Rasmus Jarlov replied that Greenlandic independence needs the Danish parliament's approval and a change to the constitution. In June 2025 Vanity Fair reported that Brown had chosen a site at Vandenberg, an American Space Force base in California, for a city called Atlas. On 22 September 2026 Praxis announced a deal to build inside +Colonia, a 515-hectare development near Colonia del Sacramento in Uruguay. The New York Times described the agreement as largely non-binding. Praxis plans to start buying land by the end of 2027, and no Praxis city has been built.
praxis.mechanism: A would-be state with no land has only a financing plan. Every possible site still needs a host government to agree.
praxis.currency: Crypto tokens linked to its financing
praxis.challenge: A Danish MP rejected the Greenland idea; a largely non-binding deal for a site in Uruguay followed in 2026
praxis.cost: $525 million reported: a conditional $500 million from GEM Digital plus $25 million

second-life-embassies.story: In 2007 a few real countries opened embassies in Second Life, an online 3D world where people move around as animated figures. Sweden announced its plan in January and was to open on 30 May with a copy of the House of Sweden in Washington, built through the Swedish Institute, a government body that promotes the country abroad, for 400,000 kronor, about $57,000. The Maldives got there a few days earlier and put its own embassy on Diplomacy Island, a virtual diplomatic quarter. Foreign Minister Carl Bildt then opened Sweden's in a ceremony held both online and in person. Estonia joined later that year, with Foreign Minister Urmas Paet citing the importance of the internet for communication and planning lectures and art shows. These countries used the embassies for publicity and cultural outreach, and the embassies added nothing to their legal status and created no territory. No report says whether any still operates.
second-life-embassies.mechanism: A recognised country's virtual presence is a way of communicating. It has no legal effect on territory or diplomacy.
second-life-embassies.recognition: Virtual embassies opened by recognised countries

tuvalu-digital-nation.story: Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 12,000 people on low-lying islands that the United Nations Development Programme classes as extremely vulnerable to climate change, and it plans to keep existing as a country online if the sea takes its land. At the COP27 climate conference in November 2022 its Foreign Minister Simon Kofe said in a video that the country would move its land, ocean and culture to the cloud, as what it called the first digital nation. The plan is to map all 124 islands and islets and to record cultural objects, language, elders' stories and dances, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them. The legal problem is that the usual test for a state requires territory. Tuvalu therefore asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries, including New Zealand and Australia, had legally recognised its digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. Australia also offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year. In its climate advisory opinion of July 2025 the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, said that the disappearance of one of a state's parts "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". The land is still there and the question has not been tested.
tuvalu-digital-nation.mechanism: Tuvalu is testing whether a recognised country stays a state after losing all its land, by asking other countries to commit to that recognition in advance.
tuvalu-digital-nation.pop: About 12,000 people in the physical country; the digital version has no residents
tuvalu-digital-nation.laws: Tuvalu's own law; it seeks recognition as a state even if its land is lost
tuvalu-digital-nation.challenge: Not tested in a dispute; a 2025 International Court of Justice opinion said losing one part of a state would not necessarily end its statehood
tuvalu-digital-nation.recognition: Law Society Journal reports 26 countries recognised its digital statehood by December 2023

wirtland.story: Wirtland was a self-declared country that existed only on the internet, founded on 14 August 2008. It called itself the first internet-based sovereign state and an experiment on whether a country can be legitimate without land. Its own announcement in 2009 claimed about 700 citizens from all five continents. It sold real objects to give itself a physical presence, including silver coins struck with its web address, stamps and a national identity card open to anyone over 18. In January 2010 a post on the international law blog The View From LL2 described a Wirtland press release proposing to ask Nauru, a small Pacific island country, to transfer a piece of its territory. The blogger noted that Nauru's recognition had gone to the highest bidder before, but said the scheme could never work and that Wirtland was no sovereign, with few citizens and no power to tax. No report says that any land changed hands, and no activity in 2026 is reported.
wirtland.mechanism: Wirtland tested whether a website could be a state, and its attempt to get land from Nauru conceded that a state needs territory.
wirtland.pop: About 700 online citizens in 2009; no one living in a place
wirtland.currency: Its own coins, including a 2009 silver piece showing a crane
wirtland.passports: A national identity card offered to applicants over 18
wirtland.challenge: No report shows the Nauru deal took place

world-service-authority.story: The World Service Authority is an organisation in Washington, DC, that issues a World Passport and other papers to people who call themselves citizens of the world. It grew from a protest by Garry Davis, a former Broadway performer and American wartime bomber pilot. On 25 May 1948 he walked into the American embassy in Paris and gave up his citizenship, saying he was a citizen of the world. That November he stormed a session of the United Nations General Assembly in Paris. In 1949 he founded the International Registry of World Citizens, and on 4 September 1953 he declared the World Government of World Citizens, with the Authority as its administrative arm. It issued passports, identity cards and birth and marriage certificates. The New York Times wrote in his 2013 obituary that over 2.5 million documents had been issued and 950,000 people registered. Supporters said the papers helped refugees and stateless people, and critics said he charged poor people for papers legally recognised almost nowhere. Foreign Policy reported that a small handful of countries accepted the passport, while the Authority claims 189 countries have at some time stamped one. Davis travelled for 65 years and was regularly arrested and expelled. He died in Vermont in July 2013, aged 91, shortly after sending passports to Julian Assange and Edward Snowden.
world-service-authority.mechanism: A document is a passport only if a border officer accepts it. The World Passport works case by case, at the discretion of each country.
world-service-authority.pop: No territory; over 950,000 registered world citizens claimed in 2013
world-service-authority.passports: The World Passport, listed by others as a fantasy document; the Authority claims 189 countries have stamped it
world-service-authority.recognition: A small handful of countries, according to Foreign Policy

freedomland-kalayaan.story: Freedomland was a territory that a Filipino businessman claimed in the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea, which the Philippines later took over and now counts as its own. Tomás Cloma owned a fishing fleet and a maritime school. His brother Filemon reportedly found the area when a typhoon pushed his boats west of Palawan in 1947. On 11 May 1956 Filemon led 40 men in taking formal possession of 53 islands and islets some 380 miles west of Palawan, and they posted a Notice to the Whole World. Tomás argued the area had no owner because Japan had given it up at San Francisco in 1951, and he declared the Free Territory of Freedomland on 21 May, with a capital on Flat Island from July. In October 1956 Taiwanese naval ships met Filemon's boat at North Danger Reef, and Taiwan later burned buildings and took property. The brothers then asked the Philippine government for support. In 1972 President Ferdinand Marcos jailed Tomás for four months for impersonating an officer by using the title admiral. In August 1974 the group adopted a new constitution and renamed the territory Colonia. That December Tomás was arrested and made to sign over his rights to the Philippines for one peso. A 1978 decree made the area the Municipality of Kalayaan.
freedomland-kalayaan.mechanism: A private claim to unowned land can become a state's claim. The Philippines cites the forced 1974 transfer as one basis for its own title, which shows how a state can take over and reuse a private occupation.
freedomland-kalayaan.stopped_by: The Republic of China (Taiwan) navy, and President Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines
freedomland-kalayaan.pop: A 40-man expedition; no lasting civilian population confirmed
freedomland-kalayaan.laws: A government named in 1956, with a capital on Flat Island; a new constitution drafted in August 1974
freedomland-kalayaan.challenge: Taiwan burned its buildings in 1956, and Cloma signed his rights over to the Philippines in 1974
freedomland-kalayaan.cost: Rights signed over to the Philippines for one peso in 1974

kingdom-of-enenkio.story: The Kingdom of EnenKio is a self-declared country claiming Wake Island, a remote Pacific atoll controlled by the United States since 1899. The Marshall Islands also claims the atoll, which it calls Ānen Kio, on the basis of oral legends and songs. In 1994 Robert F. Moore, a Honolulu resident who said he acted for a Marshallese chief, Murjel Hermios, announced that an independent kingdom existed there. It issued passports, and in 1997 the Marshall Islands Journal reported that it had declared war on the United States and was asking for Marshallese support. On 23 April 1998 the Marshall Islands government issued a formal note condemning its claims, saying its representatives were not citizens and had no right to speak for Marshallese landowners. Moore then turned to investors. He marketed $1 billion in Enenkio Gold War Bonds online, saying they were backed by gold and promising 10 percent compound interest after five years. The Securities and Exchange Commission, the American regulator of investments, said no gold or other backing existed and the bonds had not been registered as the law required. In October 2000 it won a court order from Judge Susan Mollway in Honolulu that froze his assets and required him to account for the money. No report says how the case ended, and no state recognises the kingdom.
kingdom-of-enenkio.mechanism: Ordinary American investment law stopped a claimed country's bond sale, and a real government's written denial removed the story of local authority behind it.
kingdom-of-enenkio.stopped_by: The American Securities and Exchange Commission and the Marshall Islands government
kingdom-of-enenkio.laws: Moore called himself Minister Plenipotentiary, a title for a senior envoy
kingdom-of-enenkio.challenge: A federal judge froze its founder's assets in October 2000
kingdom-of-enenkio.recognition: None; the Marshall Islands issued a formal denial
kingdom-of-enenkio.cost: A $1 billion bond offering marketed online
